claim: 17α-estradiol treatment improves metabolic parameters and slows aging in male mice.
source: 17α-estradiol treatment improves metabolic parameters and slows aging in male mice.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known finding from prior work.

claim: 17α-estradiol elicits similar genomic binding and transcriptional activation through estrogen receptor α (ERα) to that of 17β-estradiol.
source: Herein, we show that 17α-estradiol elicits similar genomic binding and transcriptional activation through estrogen receptor α (ERα) to that of 17β-estradiol.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-sequencing and RNA-sequencing data presented in Figure 1.

claim: The ablation of ERα completely attenuates the beneficial metabolic effects of 17α-E2 in male mice.
source: In addition, we show that the ablation of ERα completely attenuates the beneficial metabolic effects of 17α-E2 in male mice.
evidence: Supported by in vivo experiments in ERα KO mice shown in Figures 2-5.

claim: 17α-E2 may act through the liver and hypothalamus to improve metabolic parameters in male mice.
source: Our findings suggest that 17α-E2 may act through the liver and hypothalamus to improve metabolic parameters in male mice.
evidence: Based on inference from hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic clamp studies and hepatic analyses.

claim: 17α-E2 improves metabolic parameters in male rats.
source: Lastly, we also determined that 17α-E2 improves metabolic parameters in male rats, thereby proving that the beneficial effects of 17α-E2 are not limited to mice.
evidence: Supported by hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic clamp data in rats shown in Figure 6.

claim: ERα may be a drug target for mitigating chronic diseases in male mammals.
source: Collectively, these studies suggest ERα may be a drug target for mitigating chronic diseases in male mammals.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the findings of the study.

claim: Aging is the leading risk factor for most chronic diseases.
source: Aging is the leading risk factor for most chronic diseases, many of which are associated with declines in metabolic homeostasis (López-Otín et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to López-Otín et al., 2013.

claim: Metabolic detriments associated with advancing age are further exacerbated by obesity.
source: Metabolic detriments associated with advancing age are further exacerbated by obesity (Villareal et al., 2005; Waters et al., 2013), which has risen substantially in the older population (>65 years) over the past several decades (Flegal et al., 2010; Flegal et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations.

claim: Obesity in mid-life has been shown to accelerate aging mechanisms and induce phenotypes more commonly observed in older mammals.
source: Moreover, obesity in mid-life has been shown to accelerate aging mechanisms and induce phenotypes more commonly observed in older mammals (Bischof and Park, 2015; Horvath et al., 2014; Nevalainen et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2009; Whitmer et al., 2005a; Whitmer et al., 2005b; Dye et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations.

claim: Obesity may represent a mild progeria syndrome.
source: These observations have led many to postulate that obesity may represent a mild progeria syndrome (Salvestrini et al., 2019; Tzanetakou et al., 2012; Pérez et al., 2016; Tchkonia et al., 2010; Stout et al., 2017a).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations.

claim: Dietary interventions, including calorie restriction, can reverse obesity-related metabolic sequelae.
source: Although it is well established that dietary interventions, including calorie restriction, can reverse obesity-related metabolic sequelae, many of these strategies are not well tolerated in older patients due to concomitant comorbidities (Villareal et al., 2005; Jensen et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations and established knowledge.

claim: Compliance issues with calorie restriction remain a paramount hurdle due to adverse effects on mood, thermoregulation, and musculoskeletal mass.
source: Compliance issues across all age groups also remain a paramount hurdle due to calorie restriction adversely affecting mood, thermoregulation, and musculoskeletal mass (Dirks and Leeuwenburgh, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation.

claim: Long-term administration of 17α-E2 extends median lifespan of male mice in a dose-dependent manner.
source: The NIA Interventions Testing Program (ITP) found that long-term administration of 17α-E2 extends median lifespan of male mice in a dose-dependent manner (Strong et al., 2016; Harrison et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to ITP studies.

claim: 17α-E2 administration reduces calorie intake and regional adiposity in combination with significant improvements in systemic metabolic parameters in both middle-aged obese and old male mice without inducing deleterious effects.
source: We have found that 17α-E2 administration reduces calorie intake and regional adiposity in combination with significant improvements in a multitude of systemic metabolic parameters in both middle-aged obese and old male mice without inducing deleterious effects (Stout et al., 2017b; Steyn et al., 2018; Miller, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work by the authors.

claim: Lifelong administration of 17α-E2 beneficially modulates metabolic outcomes, including glucose tolerance, mTORC2 signaling, and hepatic amino acid composition and markers of urea cycling, which were reported to be dependent upon the presence of endogenous androgens.
source: Other groups have also determined that lifelong administration of 17α-E2 beneficially modulates metabolic outcomes, including glucose tolerance, mTORC2 signaling, and hepatic amino acid composition and markers of urea cycling, which were reported to be dependent upon the presence of endogenous androgens (Garratt et al., 2017; Garratt et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Garratt et al. studies.

claim: Multiple lifespan extending compounds, including 17α-E2, exhibit similar modifications in liver function.
source: Additionally, multiple lifespan extending compounds, including 17α-E2, exhibit similar modifications in liver function (Tyshkovskiy et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation.

claim: The lifespan-extending effects of 17α-E2 are at least associated with, if not dependent on, metabolic improvements.
source: In all, recent studies by several independent laboratories strongly indicate that the lifespan-extending effects of 17α-E2 are at least associated with, if not dependent on, metabolic improvements.
evidence: Based on inference from multiple cited studies.

claim: 17α-E2 has been postulated to signal through a novel uncharacterized receptor as opposed to classical estrogen receptors α (ERα) and β (ERβ).
source: Although 17α-E2 is a naturally occurring enantiomer to 17β-estradiol (17β-E2), it has been postulated that 17α-E2 signals through a novel uncharacterized receptor (Toran-Allerand, 2005; Toran-Allerand et al., 2002; Toran-Allerand et al., 2005; Green and Simpkins, 2000) as opposed to classical estrogen receptors α (ERα) and β (ERβ), which is due to 17α-E2 having significantly reduced binding affinity for ERα and ERβ as compared to 17β-E2 (Edwards and McGUIRE, 1980; Korenman, 1969; Littlefield et al., 1990; Anstead et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations.

claim: 17α-E2 has significantly reduced binding affinity for ERα and ERβ as compared to 17β-E2.
source: which is due to 17α-E2 having significantly reduced binding affinity for ERα and ERβ as compared to 17β-E2 (Edwards and McGUIRE, 1980; Korenman, 1969; Littlefield et al., 1990; Anstead et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations.

claim: 17α-E2 is often referred to as a non-feminizing estrogen.
source: For this reason, 17α-E2 is often referred to as a non-feminizing estrogen (Green and Simpkins, 2000; Engler-Chiurazzi et al., 2017; Kaur et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations.

claim: A novel but uncharacterized estrogen receptor, termed ER-X, may mediate 17α-E2 actions in the brain.
source: A few studies have suggested that a novel but uncharacterized estrogen receptor, termed ER-X, may mediate 17α-E2 actions in the brain (Toran-Allerand, 2005; Toran-Allerand et al., 2002; Toran-Allerand et al., 2005; Green and Simpkins, 2000), although more recent studies supporting this hypothesis are lacking in the literature.
evidence: Supported by citations, but noted as lacking recent support.

claim: No reports to date have directly tested whether the doses of 17α-E2 shown to improve healthspan and lifespan in mice are mediated through ERα and/or ERβ.
source: Similarly, no reports to date have directly tested whether the doses of 17α-E2 shown to improve healthspan and lifespan in mice are mediated through ERα and/or ERβ.
evidence: Statement about the state of the literature.

claim: ERα is a regulator of systemic metabolic parameters.
source: There is a multitude of data in the diabetes and metabolism literature demonstrating that ERα is a regulator of systemic metabolic parameters.
evidence: Based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: ERα plays a critical role in modulating metabolism in male mammals.
source: Although most of these studies have historically been performed in female mammals, more recent studies have demonstrated that ERα also plays a critical role in modulating metabolism in male mammals.
evidence: Based on recent literature.

claim: Genomic actions of ERα regulate systemic glucose homeostasis in mice of both sexes and insulin production and release in males.
source: For instance, Allard and colleagues recently demonstrated that genomic actions of ERα regulate systemic glucose homeostasis in mice of both sexes and insulin production and release in males (Allard et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Allard et al., 2019.

claim: Hepatic steatosis and insulin sensitivity, and therefore the control of gluconeogenesis, are regulated through FOXO1 in an ERα-dependent manner in male mice.
source: Other studies have also determined that hepatic steatosis and insulin sensitivity, and therefore the control of gluconeogenesis, are regulated through FOXO1 in an ERα-dependent manner in male mice (Yan et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yan et al., 2019.

claim: Hepatocyte-specific deletion of ERα was sufficient to abrogate similar estrogen-mediated metabolic benefits.
source: Furthermore, hepatocyte-specific deletion of ERα was sufficient to abrogate similar estrogen-mediated metabolic benefits (Guillaume et al., 2019; Qiu et al., 2017; Meda et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations.

claim: 17α-E2 and 17β-E2 can bind to ERα with different affinities.
source: Previous work has shown that 17α-E2 and 17β-E2 can bind to ERα with different affinities (Edwards and McGUIRE, 1980; Korenman, 1969; Littlefield et al., 1990; Anstead et al., 1997), yet potential differences in resultant genomic binding and transcriptional activity between the two ligands remains unexplored.
evidence: Supported by citations.

claim: U2OS cells do not endogenously express any form of ERα or ERβ.
source: We chose to use these cells because they do not endogenously express any form of ERα or ERβ and have been extensively utilized to elucidate the effects of ERα and ERβ agonists and antagonists on gene expression (Monroe et al., 2003; Monroe et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations.

claim: ChIP-sequencing revealed peaks of ERα genomic binding in all conditions that are qualitatively similar across treatments.
source: ChIP-sequencing revealed peaks of ERα genomic binding in all conditions, that when compared, are qualitatively similar across treatments (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: A total of 21,443 peaks were found to have a significant pairwise post-hoc comparison between vehicle and 17α-E2 and/or 17β-E2 treated cells.
source: A total of 21,443 peaks were found to have a significant pairwise post-hoc comparison between vehicle and 17α-E2 and/or 17β-E2 treated cells.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of ChIP-seq data.

claim: No statistically significant differences between 17α-E2 and 17β-E2-treated groups were observed in ERα binding.
source: No statistically significant differences between 17α-E2 and 17β-E2-treated groups were observed.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of ChIP-seq data.

claim: 17α-E2 and 17β-E2 not only induced ERα binding at the same genomic locations but also to similar magnitudes.
source: 17α-E2 and 17β-E2 not only induced ERα binding at the same genomic locations but also to similar magnitudes.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The degree of increased or decreased ERα binding was highly similar between 10 nM 17α-E2 and 10 nM 17β-E2 (Pearson's r = 0.95, p<0.001).
source: The degree of increased or decreased ERα binding was highly similar between 10 nM 17α-E2 and 10 nM 17β-E2, (Pearson's r = 0.95, p<0.001) and 100 nM 17α-E2 and 10 nM 17β-E2 (Pearson's r = 0.96, p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by statistical correlation analysis of ChIP-seq data.

claim: The degree of increased or decreased ERα binding was highly similar between 100 nM 17α-E2 and 10 nM 17β-E2 (Pearson's r = 0.96, p<0.001).
source: The degree of increased or decreased ERα binding was highly similar between 10 nM 17α-E2 and 10 nM 17β-E2, (Pearson's r = 0.95, p<0.001) and 100 nM 17α-E2 and 10 nM 17β-E2 (Pearson's r = 0.96, p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by statistical correlation analysis of ChIP-seq data.

claim: ERα-binding sites were enriched for estrogen response elements (ERE), estrogen-related receptor beta (Esrrb), and estrogen-related receptor alpha (Erra).
source: As expected, ERα-binding sites were enriched for estrogen response elements (ERE), estrogen-related receptor beta (Esrrb), and estrogen-related receptor alpha (Erra).
evidence: Supported by motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Other common motifs found within ER elements, including steroidogenic factor-1 (SF1) and motif elements of known interacting partners, including retinoid acid receptor:retinoid X receptor (RAR:RXR), were also enriched.
source: Other common motifs found within ER elements, including steroidogenic factor-1 (SF1) (Lin et al., 2007), and motif elements of known interacting partners, including retinoid acid receptor:retinoid X receptor (RAR:RXR) (Lee et al., 1998), were also enriched (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 1C and citations.

claim: Enrichment of androgen response elements (ARE) was observed in ERα peaks.
source: In addition, we observed enrichment of androgen response elements (ARE) in ERα peaks (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Many of the top enriched motifs identified contained the ERE consensus sequence TTGAC.
source: Of particular relevance, many of the top enriched motifs identified contained the ERE consensus sequence TTGAC (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by motif enrichment analysis.

claim: No differential motif binding was observed across treatment groups indicating that both 17α-E2 and 17β-E2 cause ERα to bind to the same types of genomic elements.
source: No differential motif binding was observed across treatment groups indicating that both 17α-E2 and 17β-E2 cause ERα to bind to the same types of genomic elements (Hypergeometric test, FDR < 0.05).
evidence: Supported by differential motif enrichment analysis.

claim: All samples exposed to either 17α-E2 or 17β-E2 clustered together in principle component analysis, whereas vehicle-treated cells remained distinctly separated.
source: Principle component analysis based on the entire transcriptome revealed that all samples exposed to either 17α-E2 or 17β-E2 clustered together, whereas vehicle-treated cells remained distinctly separated from treated cells on the first principle component, which explains the majority of the variance in transcription (70.6%) (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by PCA analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Treatment vs vehicle is the primary covariate explaining variance in transcriptional profiles, not the specific agonist.
source: These data suggest that treatment vs vehicle is the primary covariate explaining variance in transcriptional profiles, not the specific agonist.
evidence: Inferred from PCA analysis.

claim: No genes were found to be differentially regulated (FDR < 0.05) between the estrogen treatments.
source: No genes were found to be differentially regulated (FDR < 0.05) between the estrogen treatments.
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: Treatment of U2OS cells with either 10 nM or 100 nM 17α-E2 or 10 nM 17β-E2 resulted in nearly identical gene suppression and activation signatures compared to vehicle-treated cells.
source: Yet, compared to vehicle-treated cells, treatment of U2OS cells with either 10 nM or 100 nM 17α-E2 or 10 nM 17β-E2 resulted in nearly identical gene suppression and activation signatures (Figure 1E, left).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Both 17α-E2 or 17β-E2 treatment conditions resulted in higher ERα DNA binding affinity to gene bodies of differentially expressed transcripts compared to vehicle treatment.
source: Additionally, both 17α-E2 or 17β-E2 treatment conditions resulted in higher ERα DNA binding affinity to gene bodies of these differentially expressed transcripts compared to vehicle treatment, and no differences were observed between 17α-E2 and 17β-E2 conditions (Figure 1E, right) (negative binomial regression with Wald pairwise post-hoc).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Male WT mice displayed significant reductions in mass almost immediately after 17α-E2 treatment began.
source: Almost immediately after 17α-E2 treatment began, male WT mice displayed significant reductions in mass (Figure 2A–B) and adiposity (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: Supported by body mass data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: Male WT mice displayed significant reductions in adiposity almost immediately after 17α-E2 treatment began.
source: Almost immediately after 17α-E2 treatment began, male WT mice displayed significant reductions in mass (Figure 2A–B) and adiposity (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: Supported by adiposity data shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: Male WT mice displayed robust declines in calorie consumption during the first 4 weeks of 17α-E2 treatment.
source: Indeed, male WT mice in the current study also displayed robust declines in calorie consumption during the first 4 weeks of treatment (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by calorie intake data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: All beneficial effects of 17α-E2 on mass, adiposity, and calorie consumption were completely abolished in male mice lacking ERα (ERα KO).
source: Conversely, all these benefits were completely abolished in male mice lacking ERα (ERα KO), thereby confirming that 17α-E2 definitively acts through ERα to modulate feeding behaviors, mass, and adiposity in male mice.
evidence: Supported by data in Figures 2A-E comparing WT and ERα KO mice.

claim: Male WT mice receiving 17α-E2 displayed significant improvements in fasting insulin.
source: Similar to the mass and adiposity data described above, male WT mice receiving 17α-E2 displayed significant improvements in fasting insulin (Figure 3B), HbA1C (Figure 3C), and glucose tolerance (Figure 3D–E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), whereas male ERα KO mice receiving 17α-E2 failed to recapitulate these findings.
evidence: Supported by fasting insulin data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Male WT mice receiving 17α-E2 displayed significant improvements in HbA1C.
source: Similar to the mass and adiposity data described above, male WT mice receiving 17α-E2 displayed significant improvements in fasting insulin (Figure 3B), HbA1C (Figure 3C), and glucose tolerance (Figure 3D–E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), whereas male ERα KO mice receiving 17α-E2 failed to recapitulate these findings.
evidence: Supported by HbA1C data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Male WT mice receiving 17α-E2 displayed significant improvements in glucose tolerance.
source: Similar to the mass and adiposity data described above, male WT mice receiving 17α-E2 displayed significant improvements in fasting insulin (Figure 3B), HbA1C (Figure 3C), and glucose tolerance (Figure 3D–E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), whereas male ERα KO mice receiving 17α-E2 failed to recapitulate these findings.
evidence: Supported by glucose tolerance test data shown in Figure 3D-E.

claim: Male ERα KO mice receiving 17α-E2 failed to show improvements in fasting insulin, HbA1C, and glucose tolerance.
source: Similar to the mass and adiposity data described above, male WT mice receiving 17α-E2 displayed significant improvements in fasting insulin (Figure 3B), HbA1C (Figure 3C), and glucose tolerance (Figure 3D–E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), whereas male ERα KO mice receiving 17α-E2 failed to recapitulate these findings.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 3B-E comparing WT and ERα KO mice.

claim: Despite the masses of the male WT 17α-E2 treatment group being nearly 15 grams greater than those of the male WT chow-fed controls, glucose tolerance was essentially identical between these groups.
source: Interestingly, despite the masses of the male WT 17α-E2 treatment group being nearly 15 grams greater than those of the male WT chow-fed controls, glucose tolerance was essentially identical between these groups, thereby indicating that 17α-E2 restores metabolic flexibility in the presence of obesity in male mice (Figure 3D–E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by comparison of glucose tolerance data in Figure 3D-E.

claim: 17α-E2 restores metabolic flexibility in the presence of obesity in male mice.
source: Interestingly, despite the masses of the male WT 17α-E2 treatment group being nearly 15 grams greater than those of the male WT chow-fed controls, glucose tolerance was essentially identical between these groups, thereby indicating that 17α-E2 restores metabolic flexibility in the presence of obesity in male mice (Figure 3D–E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Inferred from glucose tolerance data.

claim: 17α-E2 failed to elicit improvements in mass, adiposity, calorie consumption, or metabolic parameters in female mice of either genotype.
source: We found that 17α-E2 failed to elicit improvements in mass, adiposity, calorie consumption, or metabolic parameters in female mice of either genotype (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: 17α-E2 significantly reduced liver mass in male WT, but not ERα KO mice.
source: We found that 17α-E2 significantly reduced liver mass and steatosis in male WT, but not ERα KO mice, as evidenced by reductions in oil-red-O positivity, fatty acid content, and triglyceride accumulation (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by liver mass data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: 17α-E2 significantly reduced liver steatosis in male WT, but not ERα KO mice, as evidenced by reductions in oil-red-O positivity, fatty acid content, and triglyceride accumulation.
source: We found that 17α-E2 significantly reduced liver mass and steatosis in male WT, but not ERα KO mice, as evidenced by reductions in oil-red-O positivity, fatty acid content, and triglyceride accumulation (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by oil-red-O, fatty acid, and triglyceride data shown in Figure 4.

claim: 17α-E2 treatment in male WT mice was accompanied by significant alterations in gene expression associated with de novo lipogenesis (fatty acid synthase [Fasn]) and β-oxidation (peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha [Pparα]; sterol regulatory element binding transcription factor 1 [Srebf1]).
source: These observations were accompanied by significant alterations in gene expression associated with de novo lipogenesis (fatty acid synthase [Fasn]) and β-oxidation (peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha [Pparα]; sterol regulatory element binding transcription factor 1 [Srebf1]) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: 17β-E2 acts through ERα to modulate the expression and activity of genes that regulate hepatic lipid metabolism.
source: These findings are similar to previous reports showing that 17β-E2 acts through ERα to modulate the expression and activity of genes that regulate hepatic lipid metabolism (Della Torre et al., 2016; Stubbins et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations.

claim: Despite seeing overall reductions in hepatic fatty acid content with 17α-E2 treatment in male WT mice, elevations in specific fatty acids were observed in these mice as compared to WT HFD controls.
source: Interestingly, despite seeing overall reductions in hepatic fatty acid content with 17α-E2 treatment in male WT mice (Figure 4C), we also observed elevations in specific fatty acids in these mice as compared to WT HFD controls.
evidence: Supported by fatty acid profile data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Arachidonic acid (AA, 20:4n6) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA, 22:6n3), both of which are precursors for eicosanoid, resolvin, and protectin production, were found to be increased by 17α-E2 treatment in male WT mice.
source: Notably, arachidonic acid (AA, 20:4n6) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA, 22:6n3), both of which are precursors for eicosanoid, resolvin, and protectin production (Szefel et al., 2015; Kohli and Levy, 2009), were found to be increased by 17α-E2 treatment in male WT mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by fatty acid profile data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and citations.

claim: The findings regarding increased AA and DHA with 17α-E2 treatment are aligned with a previous report by Garratt et al. showing that 17α-E2 increases AA and DHA in liver.
source: Our findings are aligned with a previous report by Garratt et al. showing that 17α-E2 increases AA and DHA in liver (Garratt et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Garratt et al., 2018.

claim: None of the 17α-E2-mediated changes in fatty acid profiles were observed in male ERα KO mice receiving 17α-E2.
source: None of the 17α-E2-mediated changes in fatty acid profiles were observed in male ERα KO mice receiving 17α-E2.
evidence: Supported by fatty acid profile data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: 17α-E2 treatment mildly altered several circulating eicosanoid concentrations in male WT mice.
source: We found that 17α-E2 treatment also mildly altered several circulating eicosanoid concentrations in male WT mice (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by eicosanoid data in Supplementary file 3.

claim: Many of the altered eicosanoids have been linked to changes in inflammatory signaling.
source: Many of these have been linked to changes in inflammatory signaling (Kiss et al., 2010; Gilroy et al., 2016), although the role they are playing in 17α-E2-mediated effects of on metabolism and/or aging remain unclear.
evidence: Supported by citations, but role in 17α-E2 effects is unclear.

claim: 17α-E2 reduced collagen deposition in male WT, but not ERα KO, mice.
source: Due to the association between obesity-related hepatic steatosis and the onset of fibrosis, we assessed collagen deposition by trichrome staining and found that 17α-E2 reduced this in male WT, but not ERα KO, mice (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by trichrome staining shown in Figure 5A.

claim: 17α-E2 significantly suppressed several transcripts associated with liver fibrosis in male WT mice, including collagen type 1 alpha 1 (Col1a1), cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor 1A (Cdkn1a), matrix metallopeptidase 1 (Mmp1), matrix metallopeptidase 12 (Mmp12), monocyte chemoattractant protein 1 (Ccl2), C-X-C motif chemokine ligand 1 (Cxcl1), growth differentiation factor 15 (Gdf15), and TNF receptor superfamily member 1A (Tnfrsf1a).
source: We also observed significant suppression of several transcripts associated with liver fibrosis in male WT mice receiving 17α-E2, including collagen type 1 alpha 1 (Col1a1) (Hayashi et al., 2014; Lua et al., 2016), cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor 1A (Cdkn1a) (Crary and Albrecht, 1998; Yang et al., 2020), matrix metallopeptidase 1 (Mmp1) (Lichtinghagen et al., 2003), matrix metallopeptidase 12 (Mmp12) (Madala et al., 2010), monocyte chemoattractant protein 1 (Ccl2) (Glass et al., 2018; Baeck et al., 2012), C-X-C motif chemokine ligand 1 (Cxcl1) (Yang et al., 2017), growth differentiation factor 15 (Gdf15) (Koo et al., 2018), and TNF receptor superfamily member 1A (Tnfrsf1a) (Grattagliano et al., 2019; Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 5B and citations.

claim: Transcripts shown to be predicative of hepatic insulin resistance (follistatin [Fst], inhibin subunit beta E [Inhbe], insulin receptor substrate 2 [Irs2]) and gluconeogenic plasticity (phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase 1 [Pck1], pyruvate kinase [Pkm]) were beneficially modulated by 17α-E2 in male WT mice.
source: Transcripts shown to be predicative of hepatic insulin resistance (follistatin [Fst], inhibin subunit beta E [Inhbe], insulin receptor substrate 2 [Irs2]) (Tao et al., 2018; Parks et al., 2015) and gluconeogenic plasticity (phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase 1 [Pck1], pyruvate kinase [Pkm]) (Xiong et al., 2011) were also beneficially modulated by 17α-E2 in male WT mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and citations.

claim: 17α-E2 dramatically improved phosphorylated AKT (pS473) and FOXO1 (pS256) in male WT mice treated with 17α-E2.
source: We found dramatic improvements in phosphorylated AKT (pS473) and FOXO1 (pS256) in male WT mice treated with 17α-E2 (Figure 5D–E), whereas these benefits were not observed in male ERα KO mice.
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5D-E.

claim: The benefits of 17α-E2 on phosphorylated AKT and FOXO1 were not observed in male ERα KO mice.
source: We found dramatic improvements in phosphorylated AKT (pS473) and FOXO1 (pS256) in male WT mice treated with 17α-E2 (Figure 5D–E), whereas these benefits were not observed in male ERα KO mice.
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5D-E.

claim: The findings are aligned with previous reports demonstrating that hepatic ERα plays a critical role in regulating insulin sensitivity in the liver of male mice.
source: Our findings are aligned with previous reports demonstrating that hepatic ERα plays a critical role in regulating insulin sensitivity in the liver of male mice (Yan et al., 2019; Guillaume et al., 2019; Qiu et al., 2017; Zhu et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations.

claim: The liver is highly responsive to 17α-E2 and hepatic ERα is likely the signaling mechanism by which 17α-E2 prevents and/or reverses steatosis, fibrosis, and insulin resistance.
source: Collectively, these findings suggest that the liver is highly responsive to 17α-E2 and that hepatic ERα is likely the signaling mechanism by which 17α-E2 prevents and/or reverses steatosis, fibrosis, and insulin resistance.
evidence: Inferred from the collective findings in Figures 4-5.

claim: Acute peripheral administration of 17α-E2 significantly increased systemic insulin responsiveness as compared to vehicle controls, which is indicated by increased GIRs.
source: We found that acute peripheral administration of 17α-E2 significantly increased systemic insulin responsiveness as compared to vehicle controls, which is indicated by increased GIRs (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic clamp data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Peripheral 17α-E2 administration robustly suppressed hepatic gluconeogenesis as compared to vehicle controls.
source: These studies also determined that peripheral 17α-E2 administration robustly suppressed hepatic gluconeogenesis as compared to vehicle controls (Ra; Figure 6C–D), whereas glucose disposal rates (Rd; Figure 6E) were essentially identical between groups under clamped conditions.
evidence: Supported by Ra data shown in Figure 6C-D.

claim: Glucose disposal rates (Rd) were essentially identical between peripheral 17α-E2 and vehicle groups under clamped conditions.
source: These studies also determined that peripheral 17α-E2 administration robustly suppressed hepatic gluconeogenesis as compared to vehicle controls (Ra; Figure 6C–D), whereas glucose disposal rates (Rd; Figure 6E) were essentially identical between groups under clamped conditions.
evidence: Supported by Rd data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: 17α-E2 beneficially modulates metabolic parameters independent of reductions in calorie intake and adiposity.
source: These data indicate that 17α-E2 beneficially modulates metabolic parameters independent of reductions in calorie intake and adiposity.
evidence: Inferred from acute clamp studies showing effects without long-term dietary changes.

claim: The liver is a primary site where 17α-E2 acts to improve metabolic homeostasis due to gluconeogenesis being tightly controlled by hormonal actions on hepatocytes.
source: Furthermore, these findings strongly suggest that the liver is a primary site where 17α-E2 acts to improve metabolic homeostasis due to gluconeogenesis being tightly controlled by hormonal actions on hepatocytes (Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: Inferred from clamp data and supported by citation.

claim: The hypothalamus can directly modulate gluconeogenesis in the liver through hepatic innervation.
source: However, it also well established that the hypothalamus can directly modulate gluconeogenesis in the liver through hepatic innervation (Timper and Brüning, 2017); therefore, we sought to determine if acute intracerebroventricular (ICV) delivery of 17α-E2 (Figure 6F) could modulate metabolic parameters similarly to that observed during peripheral 17α-E2 administration.
evidence: Supported by citation to Timper and Brüning, 2017.

claim: Central administration of 17α-E2 essentially phenocopied the effects of peripheral 17α-E2 infusion with regard to GIRs and suppression of hepatic gluconeogenesis.
source: Interestingly, we found that central administration of 17α-E2 essentially phenocopied the effects of peripheral 17α-E2 infusion with regard to GIRs and suppression of hepatic gluconeogenesis (Figure 6G–I).
evidence: Supported by ICV clamp data shown in Figure 6G-I.

claim: 17α-E2 likely acts through hypothalamic neurons to regulate hepatic gluconeogenesis.
source: These findings suggest that 17α-E2 likely acts through hypothalamic neurons to regulate hepatic gluconeogenesis.
evidence: Inferred from ICV clamp data.

claim: Agouti-related peptide/neuropeptide Y (AgRP/NPY) and pro-opiomelanocortin (Pomc) neurons are known to regulate hepatic glucose production.
source: Indeed, agouti-related peptide/neuropeptide Y (AgRP/NPY) and pro-opiomelanocortin (Pomc) neurons are known to regulate hepatic glucose production (Könner et al., 2007; Ruud et al., 2017; Pocai et al., 2005a; Pocai et al., 2005b; Dodd et al., 2018) and both neuronal populations express ERα (Smith et al., 2013; Skinner and Herbison, 1997; Xu et al., 2011; Acosta-Martinez et al., 2007; Stincic et al., 2018; Kelly and Rønnekleiv, 2015; Smith et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations.

claim: Both AgRP/NPY and Pomc neuronal populations express ERα.
source: Indeed, agouti-related peptide/neuropeptide Y (AgRP/NPY) and pro-opiomelanocortin (Pomc) neurons are known to regulate hepatic glucose production (Könner et al., 2007; Ruud et al., 2017; Pocai et al., 2005a; Pocai et al., 2005b; Dodd et al., 2018) and both neuronal populations express ERα (Smith et al., 2013; Skinner and Herbison, 1997; Xu et al., 2011; Acosta-Martinez et al., 2007; Stincic et al., 2018; Kelly and Rønnekleiv, 2015; Smith et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations.

claim: 17α-E2 primarily alters systemic metabolic homeostasis through the modulation of hepatic gluconeogenesis.
source: These data indicate that 17α-E2 primarily alters systemic metabolic homeostasis through the modulation of hepatic gluconeogenesis, which is known to account for 76–87% of glucose production in the body (Cherrington et al., 1994).
evidence: Inferred from clamp data and supported by citation.

claim: Hepatic gluconeogenesis accounts for 76–87% of glucose production in the body.
source: These data indicate that 17α-E2 primarily alters systemic metabolic homeostasis through the modulation of hepatic gluconeogenesis, which is known to account for 76–87% of glucose production in the body (Cherrington et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cherrington et al., 1994.

claim: 17α-E2 has the ability to cross the blood brain barrier and elicit responses in the hypothalamus.
source: Although these studies are suggestive of direct actions in the liver, 17α-E2 also has the ability to cross the blood brain barrier and elicit responses in the hypothalamus (Steyn et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Steyn et al., 2018.

claim: The suppression of hepatic gluconeogenesis by 17α-E2 is at least partially mediated by the hypothalamus.
source: These experiments essentially phenocopied the results of the peripheral 17α-E2 infusions, suggesting that the suppression of hepatic gluconeogenesis by 17α-E2 is at least partially mediated by the hypothalamus.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of peripheral and ICV clamp data.

claim: The arcuate nucleus (ARC) of the hypothalamus plays a critical role in the regulation of hepatic gluconeogenesis through autonomic regulation and vagus nerve activity.
source: A multitude of studies have shown that the arcuate nucleus (ARC) of the hypothalamus plays a critical role in the regulation of hepatic gluconeogenesis through autonomic regulation and vagus nerve activity (Ruud et al., 2017; Pocai et al., 2005a; Zhang et al., 2018; Brandt et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations.

claim: The effects of 17α-E2 on calorie intake and adiposity are dependent upon functional Pomc neurons.
source: Similarly, we have previously shown that the effects of 17α-E2 on calorie intake and adiposity are dependent upon functional Pomc neurons, thereby providing evidence that 17α-E2 can act through the hypothalamus to mediate systemic metabolic parameters (Steyn et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Steyn et al., 2018.

claim: In the absence of functional Pomc neurons, 17α-E2 was still able to reduce fasting glucose and insulin, suggesting that 17α-E2 modulates peripheral metabolism through multiple mechanisms.
source: However, in the absence of functional Pomc neurons, 17α-E2 was still able to reduce fasting glucose and insulin, suggesting that 17α-E2 modulates peripheral metabolism through multiple mechanisms, which may include alternative neuronal populations.
evidence: Inferred from prior findings cited.

claim: A recent report from Debarba et al. demonstrated that 17α-E2 increased hypothalamic ERα expression in the ARC.
source: Interestingly, a recent report from Debarba et al. demonstrated that 17α-E2 increased hypothalamic ERα expression in the ARC (Debarba, 2020), which further suggests that 17α-E2 signals through ERα in the hypothalamus.
evidence: Supported by citation to Debarba, 2020.

claim: 17α-E2 acts through ERα in the liver and/or hypothalamus to modulate metabolic parameters.
source: Collectively, our findings strongly suggest that 17α-E2 acts through ERα in the liver and/or hypothalamus to modulate metabolic parameters.
evidence: Inferred from the collective findings of the study.

claim: The findings are in contrast to other reports suggesting that 17α-E2 elicits health benefits by modulating androgen metabolism.
source: However, our findings are in contrast to other reports suggesting that 17α-E2 elicits health benefits by modulating androgen metabolism (Garratt et al., 2017; Garratt et al., 2018; Garratt and Stout, 2018).
evidence: Comparison with cited literature.

claim: Garratt et al. reported that responsiveness to 17α-E2 was significantly attenuated in castrated male mice.
source: Garratt et al. reported that responsiveness to 17α-E2 was significantly attenuated in castrated male mice (Garratt et al., 2018), which the authors proposed may indicate 17α-E2 acts as a 5α-reductase inhibitor (Schriefers et al., 1991) to prevent the conversion of testosterone into dihydrotestosterone (DHT).
evidence: Supported by citations to Garratt et al., 2018 and Schriefers et al., 1991.

claim: 17α-E2 is known to be a mild 5α-reductase inhibitor that is prescribed as a topical treatment for androgenetic alopecia.
source: 17α-E2 is known to be a mild 5α-reductase inhibitor that is prescribed as a topical treatment for androgenetic alopecia (Orfanos and Vogels, 1980).
evidence: Supported by citation.

claim: The dose of 17α-E2 used in the vast majority of these studies does not induce dramatic feminization of the sex hormone profiles in male mice.
source: However, the dose of 17α-E2 used in the vast majority of these studies, does not induce dramatic feminization of the sex hormone profiles in male mice (Stout et al., 2017b), which leads us to speculate that 17a-E2 is acting in a direct manner through ERα rather than indirectly through androgen modulation.
evidence: Supported by citation to Stout et al., 2017b.

claim: Studies in male rodents and humans demonstrate that 5α-reductase inhibition or deficiency increases insulin resistance and hepatic steatosis and fibrosis.
source: Furthermore, studies in male rodents (Livingstone et al., 2015; Dowman et al., 2013) and humans Wei et al., 2019 demonstrate that 5α-reductase inhibition or deficiency increases insulin resistance and hepatic steatosis and fibrosis, which are contradictory to the effects of 17α-E2 treatment in all of our studies utilizing male mice (Stout et al., 2017b; Steyn et al., 2018; Miller, 2020; Sidhom et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations.

claim: Several recent reports have demonstrated interactions between the androgen receptor (AR) and ERα.
source: For instance, several recent reports have demonstrated interactions between the androgen receptor (AR) and ERα (D'Amato et al., 2016; Panet-Raymond et al., 2000; Peters et al., 2009), which suggests that modulation of one may affect function of the other.
evidence: Supported by citations.

claim: It is plausible that 17α-E2 could be inducing metabolic benefits and lifespan-extending effects through several distinct mechanisms, including direct actions through ERα, suppression of DHT production, and/or aromatization of testosterone.
source: Notably, it is plausible that 17α-E2 could be inducing metabolic benefits and lifespan-extending effects through several distinct mechanisms, including direct actions through ERα, suppression of DHT production, and/or aromatization of testosterone.
evidence: Speculative statement about potential mechanisms.

claim: Constitutive global ERα KO mice have been shown to display varying degrees of compensatory ERβ activity due to the absence of ERα during development.
source: First, we utilized constitutive global ERα KO mice, which have been shown to display varying degrees of compensatory ERβ activity due to the absence of ERα during development (Sánchez-Criado et al., 2012; Rosenfeld et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations.

claim: If compensatory ERβ expression was playing a role in the study, we likely would not see a complete attenuation of 17α-E2-mediated effects.
source: However, if compensatory ERβ expression was playing a role in our study, we likely would not see a complete attenuation of 17α-E2-mediated effects.
evidence: Logical inference about the study results.

claim: ERα KO mice are known to have elevated endogenous testosterone levels.
source: Another potential concern of the model is that ERα KO mice are known to have elevated endogenous testosterone levels (Gould et al., 2007), although the studies by Garratt et al. would suggest that higher testosterone levels could potentially render the male mice more responsive to 17α-E2, whereas we observed the opposite.
evidence: Supported by citation to Gould et al., 2007.

claim: Female mice present a greater phenotypic response than males to the ablation of ERα, thereby exacerbating obesity and metabolic dysfunction.
source: However, it must also be noted that female mice present a greater phenotypic response than males to the ablation of ERα, thereby exacerbating obesity and metabolic dysfunction which makes comparisons to female WT mice as well as their male littermates problematic (Manrique et al., 2012; Vidal et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations.

claim: 17α-E2 failed to elicit beneficial responses in female mice of either genotype (WT or ERα KO), which is aligned with previous reports demonstrating a lack of effect of 17α-E2 in intact females.
source: Regardless, 17α-E2 still failed to elicit beneficial responses in female mice of either genotype (WT or ERα KO), which is aligned with previous reports demonstrating a lack of effect of 17α-E2 in intact females (Garratt et al., 2017; Garratt et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by data and citations.

claim: OVX renders female mice responsive to several of the benefits conferred by 17α-E2 treatment in male mice.
source: We also recently reported that OVX renders female mice responsive to several of the benefits conferred by 17α-E2 treatment in male mice (Mann et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mann et al., 2020.

claim: Endogenous 17β-E2 actions on ERα diminishes potential benefits of 17α-E2 in intact female mice.
source: These observations, coupled with the genomic data presented herein, support the hypothesis that endogenous 17β-E2 actions on ERα diminishes potential benefits of 17α-E2 in intact female mice.
evidence: Inferred from the collective findings.

claim: It remains unclear if metabolic improvements with 17α-E2 treatment are required for the lifespan extension effects of the compound.
source: Lastly, the current studies were relatively short in duration and it remains unclear if metabolic improvements with 17α-E2 treatment are required for the lifespan extension effects of the compound.
evidence: Statement about limitations and unknowns.

claim: Given the close relationship between metabolic homeostasis, sex hormones, and longevity, future studies evaluating the effects of ERα on male lifespan in the presence or absence of 17α-E2 will be needed.
source: Similarly, given the close relationship between metabolic homeostasis, sex hormones, and longevity (López-Otín et al., 2013; Barros and Gustafsson, 2011), we surmise that future studies evaluating the effects of ERα on male lifespan in the presence or absence of 17α-E2 will be needed.
evidence: Speculative statement about future research needs, supported by citations.

claim: The current report does not provide direct evidence that ERα modulates the lifespan extending effects of 17α-E2.
source: Although our current report does not provide direct evidence that ERα modulates the lifespan extending effects of 17α-E2, it does provide insight into the involvement of hepatic and/or hypothalamic ERα on 17α-E2-mediated metabolic effects in male mice.
evidence: Statement about the scope and limitations of the study.

claim: The data presented are the first to show that 17α-E2 and 17β-E2 induce nearly identical ERα chromatin association patterns and transcriptional activity.
source: In summary, the data presented herein are the first to show that 17α-E2 and 17β-E2 induce nearly identical ERα chromatin association patterns and transcriptional activity.
evidence: Summary statement supported by the ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data.

claim: The metabolic benefits of 17α-E2 in male mice are ERα-dependent.
source: Moreover, we demonstrate that the metabolic benefits of 17α-E2 in male mice are ERα-dependent.
evidence: Summary statement supported by in vivo data.

claim: 17α-E2 acts through the liver and hypothalamus to regulate metabolic homeostasis in male mice.
source: We also provide evidence that strongly suggests 17α-E2 acts through the liver and hypothalamus to regulate metabolic homeostasis in male mice.
evidence: Summary statement supported by clamp and hepatic data.

claim: The effects of 17α-E2 in male rats were mirrored by studies showing that 17α-E2 can modulate metabolism almost instantaneously and that these effects are not limited to a single mammalian species.
source: These effects were mirrored by studies in male WT rats receiving 17α-E2, indicating that 17α-E2 can modulate metabolism almost instantaneously and that these effects are not limited to a single mammalian species.
evidence: Summary statement supported by rat clamp data.

claim: Future studies will be needed to confirm that 17α-E2 acts predominantly through ERα in a cell-type-specific manner in the liver and hypothalamus to modulate systemic metabolic homeostasis.
source: Future studies will be needed to confirm that 17α-E2 acts predominantly through ERα in a cell-type-specific manner in the liver and hypothalamus to modulate systemic metabolic homeostasis.
evidence: Statement about future research needs.

claim: It is imperative to determine if ERα exclusively modulates the lifespan-extending effects of 17α-E2 in male mice.
source: It is also imperative that we determine if ERα exclusively modulates the lifespan-extending effects of 17α-E2 in male mice.
evidence: Statement about future research needs.

claim: Another potential avenue of investigation that remains unresolved is whether 17α-E2 acts through ERα in a genomic or non-genomic manner to modulate health parameters.
source: Another potential avenue of investigation that remains unresolved is whether 17α-E2 acts through ERα in a genomic or non-genomic manner to modulate health parameters.
evidence: Statement about future research needs.

claim: Potential interactions between androgen and estrogen signaling must be considered when evaluating the effects of 17α-E2 on metabolism and lifespan.
source: Potential interactions between androgen and estrogen signaling must also be considered when evaluating the effects of 17α-E2 on metabolism and lifespan.
evidence: Statement about considerations for future research.

claim: The studies provide critical insight into the molecular mechanisms by which 17α-E2 elicits metabolic benefits in males, which were previously unknown and may underlie its lifespan-extending effects.
source: Our studies provide critical insight into the molecular mechanisms by which 17α-E2 elicits metabolic benefits in males, which were previously unknown and may underlie its lifespan-extending effects.
